case_text:
Vignette:
A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after a skiing accident in which he sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture of the right leg, which was splinted in the field by ski patrol. He reports that his pain has been escalating dramatically despite receiving IV morphine 10 mg total, which is atypical for the degree of injury. He describes the pain as deep and burning, significantly worse with any passive movement of his right toes. On examination, the right lower leg appears tense and swollen within the splint. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 108, RR 20, BP 142/88, SpO2 99%. After splint removal, the anterior compartment of the right leg is firm and exquisitely tender. Pain is markedly worsened with passive extension of the right toes. Sensation is diminished in the first web space (deep peroneal nerve distribution). Dorsalis pedis pulse is still palpable but diminished compared to the left. Compartment pressure measurement reveals 48 mmHg in the anterior compartment (diastolic BP 88, delta pressure 40 mmHg). Orthopedic surgery is consulted for emergent four-compartment fasciotomy.
